title: ASP.NET Core 10 — what's new
exp: You're already running a .NET 10 Web API on the SCIM project — that's a talking point most candidates don't have. Know what's new so you can say "I've used X directly."
pts: **OpenAPI 3.1:** JSON Schema 2020-12 aligned. Nullable types as type arrays (["string","null"]). Better compatibility with code generators
**IOpenApiDocumentProvider via DI:** access the generated OpenAPI schema outside an HTTP request — useful in background services or startup tooling
**Automatic memory pool eviction:** ASP.NET Core's internal memory pools now release memory back to OS during idle periods
**Passkey/WebAuthn in Identity:** built-in passwordless auth using device biometrics or hardware keys — no third-party library needed
**Tighter OpenTelemetry:** more built-in meters for request duration, queue depth, active connections

qa.q: What changed about OpenAPI generation in ASP.NET Core 10?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** It now produces OpenAPI 3.1 documents conforming to JSON Schema 2020-12. Nullable reference types are represented as a type array ["string","null"] instead of {type: "string", nullable: true}. This means client generators that expect strict JSON Schema compliance now work correctly without workarounds.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** EF Core translates LINQ expression trees into SQL ASTs, executes via ADO.NET, and tracks entity state in the ChangeTracker snapshot dictionary.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** N+1 queries caused by lazy loading in loops result in hundreds of database round-trips and API latency degradation.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** AsNoTracking() boosts read performance by 20-40% and lowers memory usage, but disables automatic update tracking.

**Elevator Pitch:** A new interface injectable via DI that lets you programmatically access the generated OpenAPI document outside an HTTP request context. Use cases: startup task that uploads your API schema to an API gateway, background service that validates the schema, or integration tests that inspect the generated document without making an HTTP call.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: How would you tie .NET 10 passkey support to your SCIM/SSO project in an interview?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The SCIM system handles user lifecycle while SSO handles authentication. .NET 10's built-in passkey support means you could replace the password+JWT flow with WebAuthn using the same ASP.NET Core Identity framework you're already using — no third-party FIDO2 library. It's a direct extension of the auth work you're already doing.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** ServiceContainer tracks registration lifetimes (Transient, Scoped, Singleton). Scoped services are tied to an IServiceScope.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Captive dependencies (injecting a Scoped service like DbContext into a Singleton) cause state corruption, memory leaks, and multithreading race conditions.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Explicit scoping ensures request isolation, but requires IServiceScopeFactory for background hosted services.

interviewPlaybook.openingScript: In .NET production applications, I treat ASP.NET Core 10 — what's new as an architectural constraint where memory allocations and thread safety dictate latency SLA and process stability.
interviewPlaybook.incidentStory: In our core SaaS backend, misconfigured ASP.NET Core 10 — what's new triggered thread-pool starvation and high Gen 2 GC pauses during peak traffic. I attached dotnet-dump and dotMemory, diagnosed the allocation root-cause, refactored to zero-allocation primitives, and improved p99 API response times by 80%.
